Neonatal Brown skates (Raja miraletus) emerge from their egg cases at a total length of approximately 12.5 centimeters [Lb = approximately 12.5 centimeters], a size that is consistent with the dimensions reported for other small-bodied rajiforms in the Mediterranean basin. This measurement was derived from a series of captive-hatched individuals maintained at the Stazione Zoologica Anton Dohrn in Naples, where freshly deposited egg cases were collected from trawled adults and incubated through to hatching. The relatively modest size at birth reflects the limited yolk reserves available to the developing embryo during its protracted incubation period, which in this species is strongly temperature-dependent. Under controlled laboratory conditions held at a stable water temperature of 17.6 °C [T = 17.6 °C], the interval between oviposition and the emergence of the free-swimming pup was recorded as 5.5 months [ab = 5.5 months], a duration that aligns well with published accounts for congeners inhabiting similar thermal regimes in the Adriatic Sea. The cryptic colouration of the neonates, featuring a mottled dorsal pattern of dark spots on a sandy-brown background, provides immediate camouflage on the soft sedimentary bottoms that constitute their preferred nursery habitat, likely reducing predation pressure during the vulnerable early post-hatching phase when the pups must learn to detect and capture small benthic invertebrates.

As juvenile Brown skates grow, they undergo a prolonged period of somatic development before reaching the size threshold that triggers gonadal activation. Field surveys conducted in the Gulf of Gabès, combined with histological examination of the reproductive tracts from landed specimens, indicate that the onset of puberty in Raja miraletus occurs at a total length of 44 centimeters [Lp = 44 centimeters], a value that corresponds roughly to 55 to 60 percent of the species' asymptotic length. This pubertal size is broadly similar to that observed in other Mediterranean skate species of comparable body plan, such as Raja clavata and Raja asterias, suggesting a conserved allometric relationship between somatic growth and the initiation of gametogenesis among these elasmobranchs. Males typically reach the pubertal threshold at a slightly smaller size than females, though the difference is not statistically significant across the populations sampled. The attainment of sexual maturity is accompanied by a suite of morphological changes in the males, most notably the calcification and elongation of the claspers, while females exhibit a marked increase in ovarian follicle diameter and the development of the shell gland. Following the onset of puberty, the growth trajectory decelerates noticeably as energetic resources are increasingly diverted toward the demands of egg case production and mating behaviour.

The ultimate total length attained by adult Brown skates has been documented at 63 centimeters [Li = 63 centimeters], representing the maximum size recorded from extensive surveys of commercial bottom-trawl catches in the central and eastern Mediterranean. This asymptotic length, derived from length-frequency distributions and verified through mark-recapture studies on the Maltese continental shelf, appears to be a robust species-specific trait that is relatively invariant across the species' geographic range. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight corresponding to this maximum size is estimated at 1.45 kilograms [Wwi = 1.45 kilograms], with gravid females occasionally reaching slightly higher masses immediately prior to oviposition due to the retention of multiple egg cases within the oviducts. The length-weight relationship follows a strongly positive allometric coefficient, consistent with the dorso-ventrally flattened body morphology typical of rajiform skates, wherein width increases disproportionately with length, contributing to the substantial mass gain observed in larger individuals. These asymptotic values provide a useful reference point for fisheries managers assessing the status of Raja miraletus stocks, as they allow calculation of spawner biomass-per-recruit metrics and the estimation of size limits that protect immature segments of the population from harvest.

Reproduction in the Brown skate follows a prolonged annual cycle, with females depositing egg cases at intervals throughout much of the year in warmer regions. Under the thermal regime characteristic of their native habitat, approximately 17.6 °C [T = 17.6 °C] during the peak reproductive season, each adult female produces between 40 and 72 eggs per year [Ri = between 40 and 72 eggs per year], with a single egg case typically containing one fertilized ovum. The reproductive output is thus considerable for an elasmobranch of this body size, though it is substantially lower than the fecundity of most teleost fishes occupying similar trophic niches, reflecting the greater per-offspring investment in yolk-rich, encapsulated embryos that develop slowly over many months. Field observations suggest that individual females may deposit an egg case every several days during the height of the spawning season, with the total annual production being modulated by food availability and the female's body condition. The sex ratio among neonates in trawl surveys and laboratory hatchings is close to parity, indicating an equal investment in male and female offspring, a pattern that is consistent with the lack of any evident sexual dimorphism in adult survival rates or reproductive roles.

The maximum lifespan recorded for Raja miraletus under natural conditions is 8 years [am = 8 years], a value that was confirmed through tag-recapture analyses conducted along the Tunisian coastal shelf at a mean annual temperature of 17.6 °C [T = 17.6 °C]. This longevity is moderate for a skate of its size and places the species in a relatively fast-lived category compared to larger rajiforms such as Dipturus batis, which may live for several decades, but slower than the very small-bodied skate species that often complete their life cycles in 3 to 5 years. The natural mortality rate appears to be highest during the first year of benthic life, when the small juveniles are vulnerable to predation by demersal fishes and cephalopods, and again during the senescent phase beyond 6 to 7 years of age. The combination of a modest lifespan, a relatively early age at maturity, and the production of numerous encapsulated embryos over multiple seasons results in a population dynamics profile that is moderately resilient to fishing pressure, though localised depletions have been documented in areas where bottom trawling is particularly intense. Ongoing monitoring programmes continue to refine our understanding of the species' demographic parameters as new mark-recapture data accumulate.
